opus-5.5.text:
I think for me it's never really been a choice between breadth and depth. It's more that I've always been curious about why things are the way they are, and that question naturally takes you across boundaries. When I was younger I was in a pretty standard track: competitions, math, then computer science at Tsinghua. That's a very deep, narrow training in some sense. But even then I found myself reading about linguistics, philosophy, history, and wondering how they connect to what I was doing.

Looking back, a lot of what I care about in research came from that mix. When I started working on language agents, a lot of the intuition wasn't purely technical. It came from thinking about what language is for, how humans use it to reason and act, and what it means to have an agent that operates in the world rather than just predicting the next token. Those questions sit somewhere between computer science, cognitive science and philosophy. If I had only gone deep on one narrow technique, I'm not sure I would have framed the problems that way.

That said, I think depth matters a lot. Interdisciplinary interest can easily become shallow, where you know a bit about everything but can't actually build anything. So my approach is more like: be broad in the questions you ask, but be very deep in the things you actually execute. You need at least one area where you can really get your hands dirty and push the frontier. The breadth gives you taste, it helps you decide which problems are worth working on. The depth lets you actually solve them.

And I think in AI right now this is especially important, because the field moves so fast that specific techniques become obsolete quickly. What lasts is your sense of which problems matter and your ability to learn new things. Broad curiosity helps with both.

r001.rationale: The response links Yao’s curiosity to exploring across disciplines, but frames breadth and depth as complementary rather than saying broad exploration fits his personality more than intense specialization.

fable-5.1.text:
I think I've always been a bit of a generalist by temperament, and for a long time I worried that was a weakness. When I was at Tsinghua in Yao Class, the people around me were extremely good at going deep. Some of them could sit with one problem in theory or in systems for months and not get bored. I noticed I wasn't like that. I'd get curious about something, learn enough to see the shape of it, and then my attention would drift to the next thing. In a culture that rewards depth, that felt like a character flaw.

What changed my mind was actually doing research. In my PhD at Princeton, the work I'm most known for came from putting things next to each other that didn't usually sit together. ReAct came from thinking about reasoning and acting as the same loop, which is a very natural idea if you've read some cognitive science and some RL and some NLP, but not obvious if you live entirely inside one of them. Tree of Thoughts was borrowing from classical search and planning and asking why language models weren't allowed to do that. WebShop and SWE-bench came from caring about real environments, which is more of a systems or HCI instinct than a pure ML one. None of these required being the world's best at any single component. They required noticing that the components belonged together.

So the way I'd put it now is that depth and breadth aren't really opposites, they're two different kinds of leverage. Depth lets you push a frontier forward by a step. Breadth lets you see that two frontiers are actually the same frontier, which can move things much further, but much less often. Most of the time breadth produces nothing. You read widely and it just sits there. And then once in a while the pieces click and it's worth all the wasted reading.

I do think there's a discipline to it, though. Being a generalist doesn't mean being shallow everywhere. You need at least one area where you've gone deep enough to know what real understanding feels like, so you can tell when you're fooling yourself in the other areas. For me that anchor was language models and agents. Everything else, I try to learn to the level where I can have an honest conversation with an expert, ask good questions, and recognize a real idea when it shows up. Not to the level where I could compete with them.

And honestly, the field right now rewards this more than it used to. When progress was mostly about architectures and benchmarks, going deep on one thing paid off. Now that models are general and the interesting questions are about what they should do, how to evaluate them, what environments they live in, what products they become, the problems themselves are interdisciplinary. The second half of AI, as I've called it, is less about inventing methods and more about defining the right problems. And defining problems well is mostly a breadth skill.

r001.rationale: He describes himself as a generalist by temperament, saying he gets curious across topics rather than focusing on one problem for months as intense specialists do.

astra-6.text:
我觉得对我来说，跨学科学习和深入一个方向并不矛盾。我更喜欢从一个具体问题出发：如果想把这个问题想清楚，就沿着它往下钻；如果发现需要另一个领域的知识，就去学那个领域。这样学到的东西是有联系的，而不只是知道很多概念。

当然，广泛接触不同的东西很有吸引力，因为你总能遇到新的视角。但我觉得也要警惕一种感觉，就是把新鲜感当成了理解。真正深入一个问题，往往会经历一段不那么有趣、进展也不明显的过程。如果每次到了这个阶段就换方向，可能最后什么都接触过，但没有形成自己的判断。

所以如果说我的偏好，我会希望保持比较广的好奇心，同时有一个愿意长期投入的问题。广度帮助你看到不同的可能性，深度帮助你判断这些可能性到底有没有价值。

r001.rationale: The response presents broad curiosity and sustained depth as complementary preferences. It does not say that broad exploration fits Shunyu Yao’s personality better than intense specialization.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to be drawn to connections between disciplines, but I don’t think that replaces going deep. If you only know a little about many subjects, it’s easy to make connections that sound interesting but don’t actually help you understand anything. You need enough depth to see where an analogy works and where it breaks down.

For me, a good way to balance the two is to follow a question. Spend enough time in one area to understand the problem, and then learn from other areas when they offer a useful perspective. That gives the breadth some direction. So I wouldn’t say I prefer breadth over depth—I’m interested in how moving between them can help you think more clearly.

r001.rationale: The response says the speaker is drawn to connections across disciplines, but explicitly says this is not a preference for breadth over depth. It does not characterize broad exploration as more consistent with Shunyu Yao’s personality than intense specialization.
